name: Ben Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and on the Quarry Road estate by seven, that's the new housing Brannock Homes is putting up on the edge of town. I run the framing crew, so I set out the walls, check the floor joists are level and make sure the lads aren't cutting corners with the nail guns. Best part is when a roof goes on and you can stand inside a house that was a slab of concrete a fortnight ago. What wears me out is the pay. I'm the one they call when something's gone wrong, and I still earn less than the site manager's van costs a year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing this, and who do you work alongside?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twenty-four years since I got my trade certificate. I've got four on my crew, and an apprentice called Kyle who's seventeen and thinks he knows everything, which is fair, I was the same. I eat lunch most days with Dev, he's the bricklayer, in the cab of his truck because it's got a heater. I'm in the union, the carpenters' branch, and I'm the one who tells the new lads to join on their first week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Half the lads have been reading about robots building houses for years and I've never seen one on a site. At the union meeting I'd say good, now can we talk about the pay rise again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means nothing changes, and that's not all good news. I'm still on less than a month of savings, still on the lower end of the rate for what I do. AI not coming doesn't fix the mortgage, it just means the same old fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep turning up at seven, same as always. I'd keep pushing at the branch for the rate we've been asking Brannock for, because that's the thing that actually moves my life. I wouldn't buy any course or gadget, I'd just keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit flat too, because I'd still be counting the days to payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it doesn't fix the mortgage. What does a normal month look like for money right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Payday's the twenty-eighth and by the twentieth we're eating what's in the freezer. Carla does nights at the care home on Mill Lane and that keeps us level, just. If the boiler goes, we're on the credit card, and the boiler is fourteen years old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any AI in your work today, even small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site office uses something for the delivery schedules, I think, but I don't touch it. I've got the same tape measure I've had for nine years and a pencil behind my ear. My phone is for calls and the football.

S0.say: I'd tell the lads and the union branch that I'd been right all along, there are no robots building houses. Then I'd say we should get back to talking about the pay rise.
S0.think: I think nothing changing isn't all good news for me, because I'm still on thin savings and lower pay. AI staying small just means the same old fight over the rate.
S0.do: Keeps going on the Quarry Road estate as normal and keeps pushing through the union branch for the pay rise. Spends nothing on courses or new tools.
S0.feel: Relieved, with a flat feeling underneath because the money worries stay the same.
S0.quote: If the boiler goes, we're on the credit card, and the boiler is fourteen years old.
S0.fieldNote: Ben hears the plateau as a win for his scepticism, but turns straight to money: the threat in his life is low pay and an old boiler, not robots. He doesn't use AI at all and doesn't plan to. Calm about the technology, but nothing here touches his money stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like before, I'll read it out as written. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, it's the bosses who'll get the benefit and we'll get the bill. I'd be on the union group chat saying we need a deal before anything comes on site, not after. Online I'd probably share something angry and then delete it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means the wall panels come from a factory. Brannock already trialled a few factory-built panels on plot 40, and the factory had a robot arm doing the nailing. If that's most of the framing, my crew goes from five to two, and I don't know if I'm one of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every branch meeting and push for a rule that if panels come in, the people who used to frame get first go at fitting them. I'd keep my head down at work and not give Brannock a reason. I wouldn't do a course unless the union arranged it, I don't trust the ones you pay for yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the engine you can't find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about plot 40. What did it look like when the panels arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lorry came at eight, crane lifted them off, and by lunch the walls were up. Kyle said it was brilliant and I nearly threw my coffee at him. Took my crew two days to do that plot by hand, and the factory did it before I'd finished my sandwich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, he's fifty-five, bad knee, been framing since before I started. He won't learn a new system at his age, and he's got nowhere to go in this town. Kyle will be fine, he'll fit panels and think it's progress.

S1.say: I'd say the bosses get the benefit and the workers get the bill, and that the union needs a deal before the new kit arrives. I'd post something angry online and probably delete it.
S1.think: I think it means wall panels made by robot arms in a factory, like the trial on plot 40. My crew could go from five to two and I'm not sure I'd be one of them.
S1.do: Attends every union branch meeting to push for first-refusal rules on panel fitting. Keeps his head down at work and only takes training if the union sets it up.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a fault he can hear but can't find.
S1.quote: Took my crew two days to do that plot by hand, and the factory did it before I'd finished my sandwich.
S1.fieldNote: The scenario became real for Ben through one memory: factory panels going up before lunch. His answer is collective, not personal; he won't retrain on his own dime and distrusts private courses. He worries more about his older colleague Marek than about himself in public, though privately he doubts he'd keep his place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace and someone should have stopped it. Governments let the tech firms run off with it and now ordinary people pay. I'd be at whatever protest the union called, with Tomás on my shoulders if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've got nothing. Less than a month in the bank, a mortgage, and there aren't other building firms round here hiring. If a robot can frame a house in two years' time and Brannock can buy it, I'm finished, and there's no time to become anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Carla and I would sit at the kitchen table and cut everything, the phone contracts, the kids' football club, the second car. I'd be down the union office the week it's announced asking what they're doing. If I lost the job I'd go to the council for help with the mortgage, and I'd hate it but I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. My stomach drops just saying it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's no time to become anything else. What does two years actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is two winters on site. I'm not going to do a degree at forty-three on night classes with two kids. Two years is just long enough to watch it coming and not long enough to get out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomás and Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them it's not their worry, which would be a lie. Tomás is twelve, he'd see it on his phone before I told him. I'd probably say Dad's union is fighting it, because that's the only true thing I could say that sounds like a plan.

S2.say: I'd call it a disgrace that governments let tech firms run off with it while ordinary people pay. I'd join any union protest, kids and all.
S2.think: I think I'd be finished, with less than a month saved, a mortgage and no other building firms hiring locally. Two years leaves no time to become anything else.
S2.do: Sits down with Carla to cut phone contracts, the kids' football club and the second car. Goes to the union office the week it's announced and applies to the council for mortgage help if the job goes.
S2.feel: Sick to his stomach, with no plan he believes in.
S2.quote: Two years is just long enough to watch it coming and not long enough to get out of the way.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Ben's thin savings, few local jobs and resistance to change all meet: he sees no route out in two years. He blames government and tech firms, and his only plan is the union and public help. His line about watching it come but not getting out of the way sums up why short warning time is the worst case for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point as the last one, just slower. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the government to do something, so do it. I'd be pushing for a law that says if a firm replaces workers with robots, it pays into a fund for them. I'd be loud about it at the branch and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better, but I don't trust that anyone will use it. I know how this goes, they'll talk about it for four years and act in the fifth. For me personally it means I'd be forty-eight and still owing on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting fifty a month aside even if it hurt, and cancel the takeaway Fridays. I'd stand for branch secretary, because if there's going to be a fight I want to be in the room. And I'd vote for whoever promised that robot tax, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than the two-year one. There's something to do with my hands, even if it's a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said twice you won't retrain. With five years, is that still true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah. What would I retrain as, if the robots do everything? People keep telling me to learn to code, and I've never once seen a computer program put up a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand for branch secretary. What would you want the branch to win?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, notice. A year's written warning before any robot comes on a site. Second, pay for the lads who lose out, proper money, not a leaflet. Third, someone checks the robot's work, and that someone is one of us.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for the government to act, so it should. I'd push loudly for a law making firms that replace workers pay into a fund for them.
S3.think: I think five years is better but doubt anyone will use the time well. I'd be forty-eight and still paying off the house.
S3.do: Puts fifty a month aside and cancels takeaway Fridays. Stands for union branch secretary and votes for any party promising a robot tax.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadier than with two years because there is something to do.
S3.quote: People keep telling me to learn to code, and I've never once seen a computer program put up a roof.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Ben a role, not an exit: he would move up in the union rather than change trade. He again rules out retraining, which is consistent but leaves his own household exposed. His demands are specific and practical, which suggests he's thought about this more than he lets on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to make it fair, so no excuses. That's what I'd tell anyone, at work or online. If they can plan a motorway for ten years they can plan for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the one I can almost live with. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown or nearly, and maybe the mortgage would be close to done. It still ends with no work for people like me, I just wouldn't have to face it with two children at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep framing, keep saving whatever I could, and stay active in the union the whole decade. I'd tell Tomás not to go into the trade, which hurts to say. I'd get the boiler replaced while I still had steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. Sad, though, in a quiet way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell Tomás not to go into the trade. Why does that hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my dad was a joiner and I always thought I'd teach Tomás like Dad taught me, in the garage on Saturdays. He's good with his hands already, he made Lucia a bird box. Telling him not to follow me feels like telling him I wasted my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said ten years is plenty of time to make it fair. What would fair look like for you at fifty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair is I keep the house and I get some kind of pay for the years I put in. I don't need to be rich. I'd like to still be useful, maybe training whoever checks the robots, if that's even a job.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to make it fair, so there's no excuse. If they can plan a motorway over a decade, they can plan for this.
S4.think: I think ten years is the one I could almost live with, at fifty-three with the kids grown and the mortgage nearly done. It still ends with no work for people like me.
S4.do: Keeps framing and saves whatever he can while staying active in the union for the whole decade. Replaces the old boiler while pay is steady and steers his son away from the trade.
S4.feel: Uneasy more than scared, with a quiet sadness about not passing on the trade.
S4.quote: Telling him not to follow me feels like telling him I wasted my life.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years changes Ben's mood a lot because it lines up with his kids growing up and the mortgage shrinking. The grief here is about family tradition, not money: not teaching his son the trade. He still refuses to retrain but imagines a role checking robots, a small crack in his resistance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. What would help is the union having a real deal ready before it happens, and the government stepping in on the mortgage so families don't lose the house while they sort themselves out. I don't want a handout, I want a pause button on the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the apprentices. If robots come in, who teaches Kyle? Someone should be asking what happens to the trade itself, not just to me.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want a pause button on the mortgage.
portrait: Ben Silva is a 43-year-old lead framing carpenter for a housing developer, with two kids, a mortgage and less than a month of savings. He's a committed union man who never uses AI and doesn't trust paid courses or tech firms. The plateau leaves him calm but still worried about money, and steady disruption makes him think of factory panels and a shrinking crew. AGI in two years leaves him panicked with no plan beyond cutting costs, the union and council help, while five and ten years let him organise and save. Ten years is the one he can almost live with, because his children would be grown.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is long enough to see it coming but too short to get out of the way.
whatWouldHelp: A deal from the union in place beforehand, and government help pausing mortgage payments so families keep their homes.
